title: Italy's student and cost-of-living protests
dek: Students and cost-of-living protesters march against Giorgia Meloni's government, the clashes with police in Turin, Milan and Bologna, and the unions' call for a general strike.
summary: On Friday, October 16, students marched in dozens of Italian cities on what organisers called "No Meloni Day", protesting run-down schools, a decree capping foreign pupils at 30% of a class, the cost of living and military spending. Organisers say more than 400,000 took part; the Education Ministry puts participation in the school strike at about 1%. Police used water cannon and tear gas in Turin, and bottles and firecrackers were thrown at police in Rome.

On Saturday, October 17, cost-of-living marches called by the "Italia in Piazza" movement were held in several cities. In Milan, groups broke away and clashed with police around Piazza Duomo; Il Giorno, citing police and the prefecture, and ANSA report about 50 people detained; injury figures differ between reports. In Rome, the CGIL union held a separate rally and announced a general strike for November 20.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says the right to protest does not mean turning cities into battlefields. Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara calls the violence political hooliganism. Students and unions say the protests are about schools, wages and prices, with inflation at 4.2% in September according to Istat. Italy holds a general election next year.

Clashes resumed in Milan for a second night on Sunday, October 18, with hooded groups described by police as mostly minors from the city's outskirts looting stores including a Carrefour supermarket and a Decathlon. Police figures reported by ANSA and Fanpage differ but both describe a sharply larger toll than Saturday's, with over 270 people taken to police stations across the two days and dozens of arrests. President Sergio Mattarella called the violence unacceptable and asked for solidarity with police; on October 20 the Council of Ministers approved a decree-law sending 500 additional soldiers to Milan, though it dropped plans to give them powers of arrest. The decree, published October 22 as Decree-Law no. 190/2026, took effect October 23. It sets administrative fines of €500 to €1,000 for parents when a minor takes part in the covered offences, doubling for repeat cases, and lets prefects refer families to the juvenile court and order parents to pay for damage to public property. Accounts differ on the minimum age for a minor to be stopped or detained under the decree's public-order powers. Police searched homes in 18 cities before dawn on October 23, and heavy security deployments in Rome and Milan met a fourth round of Saturday protests on October 24 across at least eight cities. That fourth Saturday saw marches, rallies or clashes reported in at least ten cities and towns, with police carrying out more than 150 pre-dawn searches in the Milan area and opening an investigation into the movement's identified founder.

phases.name: Cost-of-living marches and the CGIL rally

events.label: reported
events.text: Farmers and truck drivers block roads in Puglia, Calabria and Sicily during the week over fuel prices, and students camp out in Milan, Rome and Bologna, AFP reports. Istat puts September inflation at 4.2%, mainly because of fuel prices.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Students march in dozens of cities on "No Meloni Day", against run-down schools, the school decree, the cost of living and military spending. Schools are occupied in several cities.

events.label: reported
events.text: Organisers say more than 400,000 young people took part, La Repubblica reports; provisional Education Ministry figures put participation in the school strike at 1.08%, Il Sole 24 Ore reports.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: In Turin, protesters throw stones and other objects at police in Piazza Castello, and police respond with water cannon and tear gas.

events.label: reported
events.text: Avvenire reports that 10 officers were injured in Turin, three minors were arrested for resisting a public official and about 50 others were identified and referred to judicial authorities.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: In Rome, thousands rally outside the Education Ministry; police say bottles, flares and firecrackers are thrown at officers.

events.label: reported
events.text: A Rome official of the Siulp police union says 18 officers were injured outside the Education Ministry, hit by firecrackers, smoke bombs, stones and bottles, and that the figure may rise, Orizzonte Scuola reports, citing ANSA. Education Minister Valditara calls the officer in charge to express solidarity.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: In Verona, police identify 21 young people and report them over criminal damage and other offences; Il Sole 24 Ore says 20 of them are under 18. Clashes are also reported in Bologna.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Meloni says she welcomes mobilisation but condemns the violence and attacks on police, and calls on all parties to back peaceful protest. Education Minister Valditara calls the violence political hooliganism, not democratic dissent.

events.label: reported
events.text: Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi says police acted decisively, professionally and prudently on a difficult day, La Repubblica reports. Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini calls students who threw stones criminals, Il Sole 24 Ore reports.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Cost-of-living marches called by the "Italia in Piazza" movement, which began on social media, are held in several cities, including Milan and Bologna; Open also lists Turin, Florence, Rome, Naples and Genoa.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: In Milan, groups break away from the march and clash with police around Piazza Duomo and the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II. Police use tear gas and a water cannon after stones and other objects are thrown; shops close and the Duomo metro station is shut.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: About 50 people are detained in Milan, almost half of them minors, according to a preliminary police and prefecture report cited by Il Giorno and to sources cited by ANSA.

events.label: disputed
events.text: Injury figures for Milan differ: Il Giorno, citing the preliminary report, says 15 members of the security forces were injured, while ANSA reports at least four officers and 20 protesters injured. Sky TG24 reports five young people taken to hospital with injuries first described as minor.

events.label: reported
events.text: In Bologna, police use a water cannon after clashes near the railway station, Reuters reports citing ANSA.

events.label: reported
events.text: ANSA, citing a police update, says 36 officers were injured or bruised in Bologna, four people, all minors, were arrested for resisting officers and seven were reported to judicial authorities.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: In Rome, the CGIL union and more than 100 associations march from Piazza della Repubblica to Piazza del Popolo. CGIL leader Maurizio Landini announces a general strike for November 20 and says more than 100,000 people took part; no independent count has been published.

events.label: reported
events.text: Opposition leaders Elly Schlein (PD) and Giuseppe Conte (M5S) attend the CGIL rally; Conte calls for the government to step down, Sky TG24 reports.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: In a social media post with video of the Milan clashes, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni says protest is a right but setting cities ablaze is not, and asks the opposition to condemn the violence without ambiguity: "every reticence becomes justification". Milan mayor Giuseppe Sala says the protesters' reasons are understandable but the violence is unjustifiable, and warns against political exploitation.

events.label: reported
events.text: Interior and justice undersecretaries from the League propose a financial deposit for demonstrations, with organisers held responsible for damage, and say an amendment is ready, Il Fatto Quotidiano reports.

events.label: reported
events.text: In Turin, young people throw objects at police guarding the entrance to Porta Nuova station and officers respond with tear gas; a group enters the Feltrinelli bookshop inside the station and knocks books to the floor, AGI reports.

events.label: reported
events.text: Bologna mayor Matteo Lepore calls the scenes near the station unacceptable and says the march did not appear to have been authorised, AGI reports.

events.label: confirmed
events.milestone: Second night of unrest in Milan
events.text: For a second evening running, hooded groups described by police as mostly minors from Milan's outskirts loot stores and clash with police around Piazza Duomo and Via Torino, two days after the October 17 cost-of-living march, Il Post and ANSA report. A Carrefour supermarket, a Decathlon store and other shops are raided, windows are smashed near La Scala, and the Duomo metro station is shut again.

events.label: disputed
events.text: Tolls for the two nights vary by outlet. ANSA, citing police sources, reports 271 people taken to police stations (220 of them minors), 32 arrests (23 minors, 13 foreign nationals), 28 people reported to prosecutors, 174 held under a new preventive-detention power, and 14 police officers injured on the Sunday. Fanpage, citing police figures, reports about 270 people stopped over the two days, 160 taken to a police station on the Sunday alone (about 80% minors), 16 arrests on the Saturday (11 of them minors), 22 people reported and 104 police officers injured on the Saturday.

events.label: reported
events.text: The Associated Press separately reports police arrested 45 people over the two nights of Milan violence, 34 of them minors, as roughly 2,000 very young people took part in the looting and clashes — a third, differing count alongside ANSA's and Fanpage's figures.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: President Sergio Mattarella says "every violence is unacceptable" and calls for "an intelligent, thorough analysis" of what he calls "unprecedented actors" behind the unrest, while voicing "full solidarity" with police, ANSA and Il Fatto Quotidiano report.

events.label: reported
events.text: Luxury boutiques including Chanel, Hermès and Pomellato shut or lower their shutters on Via Montenapoleone, fearing further unrest, ANSA reports. A newly named "Movimento 17 Ottobre" announces weekly Saturday protests in Italian cities, starting in Milan, with the slogan "until this thieving government falls"; Mayor Giuseppe Sala says the tension is not over.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Open and Avvenire report that Movimento 17 Ottobre's organisers remain anonymous, coordinating through an Instagram page and an invite-only Telegram channel (with a move to Signal under consideration) and sharing tips for hiding their identities from investigators. The group calls for a "permanent mobilisation" every Saturday at 15:00, naming Piazza Duomo in Milan, Piazza Nettuno in Bologna, Piazza Castello in Turin and Circo Massimo in Rome, plus Bari, Florence, Genoa and Padua with no square specified; Open reports the series is to start on October 24.

events.label: reported
events.text: Prime Minister Meloni chairs a public-order meeting at Palazzo Chigi, where the government says it will give a "firm" response, ANSA reports. Officials are drafting a decree-law that could extend preventive detention to up to 24 hours, including for minors, create a deferred-arrest power for group property damage, and restrict gatherings of people deemed dangerous, with a Council of Ministers meeting expected on October 20. Defence Minister Guido Crosetto says Milan would get 500 additional soldiers under the "Strade Sicure" operation, with police-type powers for about three months.

events.label: reported
events.text: Vistanet reports the draft decree-law would extend preventive detention to up to 24 hours for minors, create a deferred-arrest power allowing arrest within 48 hours for group property damage (mandatory for devastation offences during demonstrations), let police issue formal warnings to people deemed a public-order risk, create a new aggravated property-damage offence and raise penalties for blocking roads. Legislative offices were still finalising the text ahead of a Council of Ministers meeting expected that afternoon.

events.label: disputed
events.text: Accounts differ on whether the deployment of 500 additional soldiers to Milan is settled: Vistanet reports the government would reinforce the “Strade Sicure” operation with 500 soldiers given police-type powers for about three months, while Il Sud 24 reports the number was still being evaluated and the decree text was not yet complete as of Tuesday morning.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Italy's Council of Ministers approves a decree-law responding to the Milan unrest, sending 500 additional soldiers to the city under the existing "Strade Sicure" operation, Il Post and Il Fatto Quotidiano report. Plans to give those soldiers judicial-police powers, including powers of arrest, are dropped after opposition reported from the Interior Ministry and, parliamentary sources say, from the Presidency of the Republic.

events.label: disputed
events.text: Accounts differ on whether the approved decree extends preventive detention ("fermo preventivo") to minors aged 14 to 18: Il Post reports the measure is in the final text, while Il Fatto Quotidiano reports it was still undecided as the Council of Ministers met and may have been dropped after consultations with the Presidency of the Republic.

events.label: disputed
events.text: The disagreement continues after the Council of Ministers rose: Fanpage reports the minors' preventive-detention plan was dropped before the meeting over doubts about detaining a minor without parental authorisation, while Juorno reports the decree "also extends preventive detention to minors", pending the final wording due in the Gazzetta Ufficiale.

events.label: reported
events.text: Fanpage, citing Meloni's own account of the decree, reports it also creates an aggravated property-damage offence for group vandalism (fine up to €15,000 and one and a half to five years in prison) and a new offence of violently joining a group of five or more at a protest, carrying up to five years and a €20,000 fine with higher penalties if faces are covered or people are hurt; it extends the criminal-association offence to those who organise violence at marches, and makes assaults on police prosecutable without a complaint.

events.label: reported
events.text: Studenti.it reports the October 30 general strike, called by the grassroots USB union and other base unions, is going ahead as scheduled; the Collettivo Osa student group has confirmed it will join, according to ANSA, and students in Turin say they will also demonstrate that day.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: L'Unione Sarda reports the approved decree extends preventive detention ("fermo preventivo") to people who disturb public safety in crowded places, including minors, but says the power applies only from age 16; Il Post and Il Fatto Quotidiano had already reported the threshold as 14. The three outlets now agree minors are covered; they differ on the minimum age.

events.label: reported
events.text: Money.it reports the published text ties the 14-year-old threshold to a questore's gathering ban on minors deemed a public-safety risk, rather than to "fermo preventivo" itself, for which it says existing safeguards for minors remain without a new stated minimum age; it also describes a new offence of violently joining a group of five or more at a protest, carrying two to five years in prison and a €10,000 to €20,000 fine, rising to four to twelve years for organisers.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: The security decree is published as Decree-Law no. 190/2026 in Gazzetta Ufficiale no. 246 on October 22 and takes effect October 23, Il Sole 24 Ore and Scuola Informa report. Parents face an administrative fine of €500 to €1,000, doubling for repeat cases, when a minor takes part in the covered offences, unless they show they could not have prevented it; prefects can refer families to the juvenile court and order parents to pay for damage to public property, which parents can contest within 40 days before the local court.

events.label: reported
events.text: Police search homes across 18 Italian cities before dawn, targeting about 100 people identified during the previous week's unrest, half of them minors, and seize phones, weapons, protective gear and goods allegedly stolen in looting, ANSA reports. Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi says investigators are starting to "peel back" the phenomenon and that there was "certainly coordination" among participants, though he will not say whether anyone directed it.

events.label: reported
events.text: ANSA reports police uncovered an online chat group in Crema organising patrols against foreign residents, run by a 20-year-old with previous convictions.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Italy deploys roughly 1,500 police in Rome and about 1,800 security personnel in Milan, including 500 soldiers, with drones and Carabinieri aircraft overhead, as Movimento 17 Ottobre holds a fourth round of Saturday protests in at least eight cities, Euronews and AFP report. Milan bars protests from the Duomo, Garibaldi and Porta Venezia districts; more than 30 mobilisations are planned nationwide.

events.label: reported
events.text: Movimento 17 Ottobre cancels the squares it had previously announced, saying it will instead name three gathering points at 2:30pm local time in each city, followed an hour later by a final assembly point, ANSA reports. Milan mayor Giuseppe Sala urges shops to stay open, saying "if panic spreads then everything stops," and says the city will simply field more officers than last weekend, AFP reports.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Italy holds a fourth round of nationwide protests called by Movimento 17 Ottobre, with marches or rallies reported in at least ten cities including Rome, Milan, Turin and Bologna, Euronews and Il Sole 24 Ore report.

events.label: confirmed
events.text: Police carry out more than 150 searches before dawn in Milan, Monza and about 20 other towns, mainly in Lombardy, targeting people identified during the previous weekend's unrest, Euronews and Il Sole 24 Ore report.

events.label: reported
events.text: In Turin, police make a tactical charge and officers throw dispersal devices after demonstrators throw objects and firecrackers; two people are detained for questioning, and protesters burn a photograph of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni in Piazza Castello, Il Sole 24 Ore reports.

events.label: reported
events.text: In Rome, demonstrators enter the Colosseum and have a tense encounter with its security staff before leaving and facing police outside; a separate march under the banner "Keep Italy out of the war" protests military spending, Il Sole 24 Ore reports.

events.label: reported
events.text: In Bologna, about 1,000 people gather in Piazza del Nettuno and several hundred clash with police at close quarters. In Milan, an antifascist march sets off from Piazza Castello and a roughly 600-strong, mostly student march leaves the Politecnico after an earlier 500-person pro-Palestinian rally; some shops close. Marches of a few hundred to about 1,000 people are also reported in Genoa, Florence, Naples and Perugia, Il Sole 24 Ore reports.

events.label: reported
events.text: In Castel Volturno, near Naples, religious groups, charities, migrant organisations and agricultural workers back a protest against a planned 120-place migrant detention and repatriation centre, with thousands expected, Euronews and Il Sole 24 Ore report.

events.label: reported
events.text: Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi writes on social media that there will be "no safe havens" for anyone organising attacks or riots. Il Sole 24 Ore reports that the alleged founder of Movimento 17 Ottobre has been placed under investigation for incitement over the group's Instagram and Telegram accounts.

events.label: pending
events.text: A reconciled national total of arrests, detentions and injuries from the October 24 protests; the outcome in Castel Volturno and any further unrest later Saturday; the investigation into the group's alleged founder; turnout on the October 30 strike; the CGIL's general strike called for November 20; and whether Parliament converts Decree-Law no. 190/2026 into law within 60 days. Still being checked.

events.label: reported
events.text: A Milan judge orders the release of the alleged administrator of the Movimento 17 Ottobre Telegram group, held since October 24 on suspicion of incitement, saying there are no serious grounds to believe he committed the offences; Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni calls the decision "shameful", Reuters reports. The court's president calls her remarks "unacceptable".

events.label: reported
events.text: The government announced it will deploy 500 army troops to assist police in Milan through the end of the year, and introduced new penalties that hold parents financially liable for children who commit vandalism, NBC News reports.

events.label: reported
events.text: The Unione Sindacale di Base and other trade unions called for a nationwide strike of public and private sector workers, NBC News reports.

claims.title: What are the protests about?
claims.label: disputed
claims.a: The government condemns the violence. Meloni says she welcomes peaceful mobilisation; Valditara calls the violence political hooliganism with nothing to do with students' rights, and Tajani accuses part of the opposition of fuelling the unrest.
claims.b: Students and unions say the protests are about crumbling schools, the school decree, low wages, rising prices and military spending. The CGIL says Italy is in a dramatic economic and social crisis.
claims.status: Open. Both positions are on record.

claims.title: How many took part on October 16?
claims.label: disputed
claims.a: Organisers say more than 400,000 young people marched.
claims.b: Provisional Education Ministry figures put participation in the school strike at 1.08%.
claims.status: The two figures measure different things (marchers and striking school staff and students), and no independent count of marchers has been published.

corrections.text: An earlier version said police made seven arrests in Bologna, as Reuters reported citing ANSA. A later ANSA report, citing police, says four people were arrested and seven reported to judicial authorities; the item has been updated.
Earlier entries named a private individual who was placed under investigation; the name has been removed in line with our policy of not naming people accused of offences.
